The theme song from the movie *Arthur* is performed by **Christopher Cross**.  
The single was issued on **Warner Bros. Records**, which is a subsidiary of **Warner Music Group** (WMG).

**Owner of the label**

*Warner Music Group* is majority‑owned by **Access Industries** (72 % equity, 98 % voting power).  
Access Industries is controlled by **Len Blavatnik** (founder of the conglomerate).

| Warner Music Group | Access Industries | 72 % of shares, 98 % of votes |
| Access Industries | Len Blavatnik | Founder and controlling stakeholder |

**Sources**

* Christopher Cross – “Arthur’s Theme (Best That You Can Do)” is a single by Cross released on Warner Bros. Records【6†L43-L51】.  
* Warner Music Group – The company’s owner is Access Industries, which holds 72 % equity and 98 % voting power【5†L20-L26】.  
* Access Industries – Founded and led by Len Blavatnik【5†L12-L18】.

So, the owner of the record label that Christopher Cross (the singer of the *Arthur* theme song) is part of is **Len Blavatnik**, via his holding company Access Industries.

Musical artist

**Christopher Charles Geppert** (born May 3, 1951), known professionally as **Christopher Cross,** is an American singer, songwriter, and [guitarist]. He won five [Grammy Awards] for his [eponymous debut album] "Christopher Cross (album)") released in 1979. The singles "[Sailing] "Sailing (Christopher Cross song)")" (1980), and "[Arthur's Theme (Best That You Can Do)] "Arthur's Theme (Best That You Can Do)")", from the 1981 film [_Arthur_] "Arthur (1981 film)"), peaked at number one on the U.S. [_Billboard_ Hot 100].[[1]][[2]][[3]]

"Sailing" earned three Grammys in 1980.[[4]] "Arthur's Theme" won in 1982 the [Oscar] for [Best Original Song], with co-writers [Burt Bacharach], [Carole Bayer Sager], and [Peter Allen] "Peter Allen (musician)").

## Early life

[[edit]]

Christopher Charles Geppert was born on May 3, 1951 in [San Antonio], Texas. A self-described "[army brat]", Cross is the son of a U.S. Army [pediatrician] who was stationed at [Walter Reed Army Hospital] in Washington, D.C., in the mid-1950s and acted as a physician for President [Dwight Eisenhower]'s grandchildren.[[5]] He attended [Alamo Heights High School] in [San Antonio], graduating in 1969. He played football and participated in track and field.[[6]] Cross was raised Catholic.[[7]]

## Career

[[edit]]

### Early musical career

[[edit]]

Geppert developed an early interest in music, citing the influence of Buddy Holly, Ritchie Valens, and Dave Brubeck during childhood.[[8]] As a seventh grader, he received a drum kit and began performing in a band called the Psychos, which played local church events and junior high school dances.[[8]] Initially serving as the group’s drummer, Geppert also took on vocal duties due to the absence of another singer.[[8]]

During high school, he shifted his primary focus to guitar, which he found more conducive to songwriting.[[8]] Around this time, he became influenced by [Frank Zappa], whom he admired less for Zappa's eccentricity and more for his instrumental approach and innovative rhythmic ideas.[[8]]

Geppert, bassist Andy Salmon, and keyboardist Rob Meurer met in San Antonio when they were still teens. Geppert and Salmon became bandmates in Flash, with Geppert on guitar. Together, they formed Christopher Cross as a band and moved to Austin, where they added drummer [Tommy Taylor] "Tommy Taylor (drummer)"). There, they played covers for cash while recording demo versions of original songs at Austin's Odyssey Sound, which later became Pecan Street Studio, which they shipped to record labels.[[9]][[10]] Though they considered themselves a band, [Warner Bros.] signed Christopher Cross as a solo artist in early 1979.[[9]][[10]][[11]]

Although best known for his vocals and songwriting, Cross is also a skilled guitarist. [Donald Fagen] and [Walter Becker] of [Steely Dan] invited Cross to play on their albums, but Cross declined because "he was so intimidated, afraid to do it."[[12]] Cross also substituted for [Ritchie Blackmore] during a [Deep Purple] concert in 1970 in San Antonio when Blackmore fell ill, and a local promoter recommended Cross as a last-minute replacement.[[10]][[13]]

Cross was the original owner of fellow Austin guitarist [Stevie Ray Vaughan]'s "Number One" 1962/1963 hybrid [Fender Stratocaster]. Vaughan purchased the guitar at Ray Hennig's Heart of Texas Music in Austin in 1974, only one day after Cross had traded the guitar for a [Gibson Les Paul].[[14]]

### First album and immediate success

[[edit]]

Cross released his self-titled debut album, _[Christopher Cross] "Christopher Cross (album)")_, on December 27, 1979.[[15]][_Billboard_ Hot 100] top 20 hits from this album included "[Ride Like the Wind]" (featuring backing vocals by [Michael McDonald] "Michael McDonald (singer)")), "[Sailing] "Sailing (Christopher Cross song)")", "[Never Be the Same] "Never Be the Same (Christopher Cross song)")" and "[Say You'll Be Mine] "Say You'll Be Mine (Christopher Cross song)")" (featuring backing vocals by [Nicolette Larson]). "Ride Like the Wind" hit number two on the U.S. Hot 100, while "Sailing" topped the chart for one week.[[1]] "Never Be The Same" went number one on the Adult Contemporary chart. Cross, the album, and the song "Sailing" were nominated for six Grammy Awards in 1980 and won five.[[16]]

Cross was the first artist in Grammy history to win all four general field awards in a single ceremony, bringing home [Record of the Year] ("Sailing"), [Album of the Year] (_Christopher Cross_), [Song of the Year] ("Sailing") and [Best New Artist] at the [23rd Annual Grammy Awards].[[a]] This feat was not replicated for 39 years, until [Billie Eilish] won all four awards at the [62nd Annual Grammy Awards] in 2020.

"**Arthur's Theme (Best That You Can Do)**" is a song performed and co-written by American singer-songwriter [Christopher Cross] as the main theme for the 1981 film _[Arthur] "Arthur (1981 film)")_.

It was recognized as the year's Best Original Song at both the [54th Academy Awards] and [39th Golden Globe Awards].[[3]]#cite_note-British_Hit_Singles_&_Albums-3)

A commercial success in the United States, it reached the top of both the [_Billboard_ Hot 100] and [Hot Adult Contemporary] "Adult Contemporary (chart)") charts in October 1981, remaining at the top of the Hot 100 for three consecutive weeks. The song topped the [VG-lista] chart in Norway and was a top-ten hit in several other countries.

## Background

[[edit]&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

The song was written in collaboration between Cross, [Burt Bacharach], and Bacharach's frequent writing partner and future wife [Carole Bayer Sager]. A fourth writing credit went to [Liza Minnelli]'s ex-husband, Australian songwriter [Peter Allen] "Peter Allen (musician)"),[[3]]#cite_note-British_Hit_Singles_&_Albums-3) a frequent collaborator with Bayer Sager. The line in the chorus "When you get caught between the moon and New York City" was taken from an unreleased song written by Allen and Bayer Sager.[[4]]#cite_note-4) Allen came up with the line while his plane was in a holding pattern during a night arrival at [John F. Kennedy International Airport].[[5]]#cite_note-5) The song also features [Toto] "Toto (band)") members [Steve Lukather], [Jeff Porcaro] and [David Hungate].

## Release

[[edit]&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Release")]

The song "Minstrel Gigolo" served as the record's [B-side], having previously backed Cross's debut single, "[Ride Like the Wind]".

Cross included "Arthur's Theme (Best That You Can Do)" as a bonus track exclusive to cassette and CD versions of his 1983 album _[Another Page]_.

## Music video

[[edit]&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Music video")]

The [music video] consists of two acts, which are edited together in fade outs. In one, Christopher Cross performs the song with musicians in a recording studio, and the other is the story the song illustrates.

## Reception

[[edit]&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Reception")]

The song won an [Academy Award for Best Original Song] at the [54th Academy Awards]. The song was also recognized as the year's Best Original Song at the [39th Golden Globe Awards].

The song ranked No. 79 among the [AFI's 100 Years...100 Songs] survey in 2004.
